k: A sample of constant composition: a single element or compound
Two or more substances combined, either homogeneous or heterogeneous
A property that depends on the amount of sample, like mass or volume
A property independent of sample amount, like density or boiling point
Mass per unit volume of a substance
units.title: Matter & measurement
notes: Classify a sample before calculating: a pure substance has fixed composition; a mixture can vary. A compound contains more than one element chemically combined.
A physical change keeps chemical identity. A chemical change creates different substances. A property describes what a sample is like or how it can behave.
Mass and volume depend on sample size. Density and boiling point are intensive when conditions and composition are fixed.
Write conversion factors so unwanted units cancel. For squared or cubed units, apply the conversion factor to the same power.
method: Identify the requested unit.
Write a chain of unit ratios.
Calculate and check the scale.
units.trap: Do not use the final water level as an object’s volume: use the rise in water level.
units.label: Lecture 2

units.t: Measurement, Significant Digits, and Problem Solving
k: All certain digits in a measurement plus one estimated digit
How close a measurement is to the true value
How close repeated measurements are to one another
Using conversion factors to cancel units and reach the desired unit
f: Sig figs in addition and subtraction
Result has as many decimal places as the least precise value
Sig figs in multiplication and division
Result has as many significant figures as the value with the fewest
units.title: Precision & significant figures
notes: A measured value contains certain digits plus one estimated digit. Exact counts and defined conversion factors do not limit precision.
Leading zeros do not count. Zeros between nonzero digits count; trailing zeros after a decimal point count. Scientific notation makes intended precision explicit.
For products and quotients, use the fewest significant figures. For sums and differences, use the least precise decimal place.
Keep guard digits through intermediate steps. Round the final answer once. Accuracy concerns agreement with a reference; precision concerns agreement among repeated results.
method: Choose the appropriate rounding rule.
Compute without rounding intermediate steps.
Report the final value at the required precision.
units.trap: Kelvin has no degree symbol. The exact offset 273.15 does not add precision to a measured Celsius temperature.
units.label: Lecture 3

units.t: Atomic Theory, Atomic Structure, and the Periodic Table
k: A compound always contains the same elements in the same mass proportions
Masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of another form small whole-number ratios
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
A horizontal row of the periodic table
A vertical column of the periodic table
units.title: Atoms, ions & the periodic table
notes: Atomic number Z counts protons and identifies the element. Mass number A counts protons plus neutrons in one isotope.
Isotopes have the same Z and different neutron counts. Ions form by changing electron count, not proton count.
For a charge written as a signed number, electrons = Z − charge. A negative charge therefore means more electrons than protons.

The periodic table groups elements with related chemistry. Groups run vertically; periods run horizontally. Definite proportions concerns one compound; multiple proportions compares different compounds of the same elements.
method: Find Z from the element.
Calculate neutrons as A − Z.
Adjust electron count for the signed charge.
units.trap: Mass number is an integer count. Isotopic mass in u is close to that count, but is not exactly the same quantity.
units.label: Lecture 4

units.t: Atomic Mass, Isotopes, and Chemical Formulas
k: Mass averaged over isotopes, weighted by natural abundance
Gives the type and number of every atom in a molecule
Gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms
Shows how the atoms are connected
Different molecules sharing the same molecular formula
units.title: Isotopes & chemical formulas
notes: An average atomic mass is a weighted mean of isotope masses. Use fractional abundances that add to 1.
For two isotopes, write the fractions as x and 1 − x. For several isotopes, subtract known percentages from 100% to find a missing abundance.
A molecular formula gives actual atom counts; an empirical formula gives the smallest whole-number ratio. A structural formula records connections.
Constitutional isomers have the same molecular formula and different connectivity. Matching a formula alone does not establish identical structure.
method: Convert percentages to fractions.
Multiply each mass by its fraction and add.
Check that the mean lies between the isotope masses.
units.trap: Do not round an average atomic mass to an integer before using it in a molar-mass calculation.
units.label: Lecture 5

k: An ion made of a single atom, such as Ca²⁺ or Cl⁻
An ion made of several bonded atoms, such as SO₄²⁻
Electrically neutral material made of cations and anions in a repeating structure
Compound of nonmetals held together by covalent bonds
An acid that contains an oxyanion
f: Show the charge of a metal that can form more than one ion
H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂
units.title: Compounds & naming
notes: An ionic formula must have total charge zero. Choose the smallest whole-number ratio of ions and place parentheses around a repeated polyatomic ion.
Name ionic compounds as cation then anion. A Roman numeral gives a variable-charge metal’s charge, not its subscript. Ammonium salts are ionic even though they contain no metal.
For molecular compounds, prefixes state atom counts. Usually omit mono- on the first element. Familiar acid names follow their own rules.
An -ate oxyanion gives an -ic acid; -ite gives -ous. Binary acids in water use hydro-…-ic acid. Not every ionic solid is soluble.
method: Identify ionic, molecular, or acid naming.
Find ion charges or atom counts.
Check charge balance and parentheses.
units.trap: Do not use molecular prefixes to name an ionic compound, or infer that every metal must have a Roman numeral.
units.label: Lecture 6

units.t: Moles, Formula Masses, and Formula Determination
k: SI amount of substance containing exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities
Mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol
Percent by mass of each element in a compound
Burning a sample and measuring CO₂ and H₂O to find its C and H content
f: % X = (mass of X ÷ mass of compound) × 100%
Multiply the empirical formula by (molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass)
n = m / M (M is molar mass)
units.title: Moles & formula determination
notes: Use molar mass to move between grams and moles. Use Avogadro’s constant to move between moles and entities; specify whether you mean atoms, molecules, or formula units.
Mass percent is the mass contributed by one element divided by the compound’s total mass. For percentages, a hypothetical 100 g sample is a convenient starting point.
To find an empirical formula, convert each element’s mass to moles, divide by the smallest, then scale all ratios to whole numbers. A ratio near 1.5 usually calls for multiplying all ratios by 2.
Combustion analysis gives n(C) = n(CO₂) and n(H) = 2n(H₂O). If a sample contains only C, H, and O, find its oxygen mass by subtracting C and H masses from the sample mass.
method: Masses → moles of each element.
Moles → smallest whole-number ratio.
Use molar mass to scale to the molecular formula.
units.trap: A formula such as H₂O counts atoms per molecule; one mole of H₂O contains two moles of H atoms.
units.label: Lecture 7

k: The component that does the dissolving, usually in greater amount
A component dissolved in the solvent
A solution with water as the solvent
Moles of solute per liter of solution
f: % m/v = g solute per 100 mL of solution
units.title: Solutions & concentration
notes: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of final solution. It is not moles per liter of solvent added.
During dilution, solute amount stays constant: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. Use matching volume units on both sides.
Mass percent uses mass of solution in the denominator; volume percent uses solution volume. A mass/volume percentage states grams of solute per 100 mL of solution.
Density can connect mass of solution to volume of solution. For an ionic solute, multiply the formula-unit concentration by the number of each ion released.
method: Convert volume to liters when using n = MV.
Find solute moles.
Divide by final solution volume.
units.trap: Final volume and solvent added are different. Subtract the initial volume only when volume additivity is explicitly assumed.
units.label: Lecture 8

k: A species used up in a reaction
A species formed in a reaction
A number in front of a formula giving the ratio of species in a reaction
Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so equations must balance
units.title: Balancing reactions
notes: A balanced reaction conserves each element and total charge. Coefficients count relative numbers of entities or moles.
Change coefficients in front of formulas; never change a formula’s subscripts to balance an equation.
Balance elements present in the fewest species first. An unchanged polyatomic ion can sometimes be counted as one unit.
For combustion of a C/H/O compound, balance carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen. Clear fractional coefficients at the end and reduce to the smallest integers.
method: Write correct reactant and product formulas.
Adjust coefficients and recount every element.
Reduce to the smallest whole-number set.
units.trap: A mole ratio is not a mass ratio. Species with different molar masses need different masses for equal moles.
units.label: Lecture 8

k: Reaction in solution that produces a poorly soluble solid
Ions that appear unchanged on both sides of a reaction
Equation showing only the species that actually react
Point at which reactants have combined in the balanced reaction’s stoichiometric ratio
f: Oxidation state of a free element
They sum to the overall charge
Usually O = −2 and H = +1; bonded F = −1. Apply exceptions when specified.
n(A)/a = n(B)/b for balanced coefficients a and b
units.title: Aqueous reactions & redox
notes: Use solubility rules to predict a solid product. Group 1 and ammonium salts, and nitrates, are generally soluble. The reference panel includes the course’s qualitative solubility table.
For a net ionic equation, split strong aqueous electrolytes into ions. Keep solids, liquids, gases, and weak electrolytes intact. Cancel only species that are identical on both sides.
Neutralization follows the balanced reaction. Equivalence means stoichiometric amounts have reacted; acid and base moles are equal only for a 1:1 reaction.
Oxidation increases oxidation state; reduction decreases it. The reducing agent is oxidized, and the oxidizing agent is reduced. Oxidation states are bookkeeping, not necessarily real atomic charges.
method: Predict products and physical states.
Balance atoms and charge.
Cancel spectator ions or track oxidation-state changes.
units.trap: The familiar O = −2 and H = +1 assignments have exceptions. A question must give enough context to recognize the relevant rule.
units.label: Lecture 9

k: The quantitative relationship between amounts of reactants and products
The reactant that is completely used up first
A reactant left over after the limiting reactant is consumed
Ratio of coefficients used as a conversion factor
f: grams A → mol A → mol B (coefficient ratio) → grams B
Smallest available n / stoichiometric coefficient limits the reaction
units.title: Stoichiometry & limiting reactants
notes: A balanced equation supplies mole ratios. Convert a given mass to moles before applying those ratios.
For each reactant, divide its available moles by its coefficient. The smallest value sets the maximum reaction amount.
Calculate theoretical product from the limiting reactant. To find excess remaining, subtract the amount consumed from its initial amount.
For solutions, first use n = MV. After reaction, compute any remaining concentration using the final mixed volume, if the problem says volumes add.
method: Find each reactant’s moles.
Compare moles divided by coefficient.
Use the limiting amount to find products and leftovers.
units.trap: The smallest starting mass is not necessarily the limiting reactant.
units.label: Lecture 10

k: Maximum product possible if all of the limiting reactant reacts
The amount of product actually obtained
Actual yield as a percentage of theoretical yield
Adding one reactant to another in small measured amounts to follow the reaction
The reactant of unknown concentration in a titration
The reactant added slowly from the buret
A substance that changes color near the equivalence point
units.title: Yield & titrations
notes: Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reactant. Actual yield is measured. Percent yield compares actual to theoretical amounts in the same units.
For consecutive reaction steps, multiply fractional yields. An 80% step followed by a 75% step gives 60% overall yield.
At titration equivalence, n(A)/a = n(B)/b for the balanced coefficients a and b. An indicator endpoint is an observed signal close to that ideal point.
Titration can reveal concentration, mass percent, or molar mass. For a known acid mass, find acid moles from titrant moles and the neutralization ratio.
method: Balance the reaction.
Use the known titrant to find analyte moles.
Convert those moles to the quantity requested.
units.trap: Do not apply MₐVₐ = MᵦVᵦ without first checking the reaction coefficients.
units.label: Lecture 11

k: The study of heat absorbed or released in reactions and processes
The system absorbs heat from its surroundings (q > 0)
The system releases heat to its surroundings (q < 0)
The total microscopic kinetic and potential energy of a system
Heat needed to change a sample’s temperature by 1 °C
Heat needed to change 1 g of a substance by 1 °C
units.title: Energy, heat & work
notes: Choose the system first. Heat entering it is positive; heat leaving it is negative. Work done on the system is positive; work done by it is negative.
The first law is ΔU = q + w. For expansion or compression against a constant external pressure, w = −PextΔV.
Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Temperature is not a measure of a sample’s total stored energy.
For a sample with approximately constant specific heat and no phase change, q = mcΔT. A sample’s heat capacity is C = mc.
method: Define the system and signs.
Put heat and work in matching units.
Add q and w or apply q = mcΔT.
units.trap: Expansion gives negative work; compression gives positive work. Convert L·atm to J before adding work to heat in joules.
units.label: Lecture 12

k: Measuring heat of a process from the temperature change of a calorimeter
Coffee-cup calorimetry; the vessel is not sealed
Calorimetry in a rigid vessel; the volume stays fixed
Reaction with an oxidant, commonly oxygen, that releases energy
f: qrxn = −(msolution csolution + Ccup)ΔT; omit Ccup only if neglected
units.title: Calorimetry
notes: For an insulated setup, the heat changes of system and surroundings sum to zero. If the solution warms, the reaction releases heat.
For coffee-cup measurements, qsolution = msolution csolution ΔT. Include calorimeter heat capacity if it is given; otherwise follow the stated neglect assumption.
At constant pressure, measured heat corresponds to ΔH when only pressure–volume work occurs. At constant volume, heat corresponds to ΔU when no other work occurs.
For a hot solid placed in cooler water, use a common final temperature and separate temperature changes: qmetal + qwater = 0, neglecting the cup and environmental loss.
method: Calculate the surroundings’ heat gain or loss.
Reverse the sign to get the reaction heat.
Divide by moles if a molar quantity is requested.
units.trap: A sealed vessel is not automatically rigid. The bomb’s fixed volume, rather than the seal alone, is what makes it constant-volume calorimetry.
units.label: Lecture 13

k: H = U + PV; ΔH equals constant-pressure heat when only pressure–volume work occurs
A property that depends only on initial and final states, not the path
Enthalpy change for forming one mole of a substance from reference-state elements
The ΔH of an overall reaction equals the sum of the ΔH of its steps
f: Multiplies ΔH by the same factor
units.title: Enthalpy & Hess’s law
notes: Enthalpy is H = U + PV. At constant pressure with only pressure–volume work, ΔH equals the heat transferred. H and U are state functions; heat and work depend on the path.
Reversing a reaction changes the sign of ΔH. Multiplying all coefficients multiplies ΔH by the same factor.
Hess’s law adds enthalpy changes for reactions that sum to the target reaction. Cancel intermediate species and check physical states.
Formation enthalpy describes making one mole from elements in their reference states. Use ΔH°rxn = ΣνΔH°f(products) − ΣνΔH°f(reactants). A reference-state element has ΔH°f = 0.
method: Match species, coefficients, and phases.
Reverse or scale the given reactions.
Add enthalpies after canceling intermediates.
units.trap: Liquid water and water vapor have different formation enthalpies. Standard state specifies reference conditions; temperature must still be stated (often 298.15 K).
units.label: Lecture 14

units.t: Electromagnetic Energy and the Bohr Model
k: Distance between successive crests of a wave
Number of wave cycles per second
A particle of light with energy proportional to its frequency
Light ejecting electrons from a metal if its frequency exceeds a threshold
Lowest-energy state of an atom; for hydrogen, its electron has n = 1
A state above an atom’s minimum energy; for hydrogen, the electron has n > 1
units.title: Light & the hydrogen atom
notes: For light in vacuum, c = λν and photon energy E = hν. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength and more energy per photon.
In the photoelectric effect, each electron receives energy from a photon. Above threshold, KEmax = hν − Φ. Greater intensity increases photon count; it does not increase energy per photon.
Hydrogen energy levels follow Eₙ = −RH/n². Absorption raises the atom’s energy; emission lowers it. The photon always carries a positive energy magnitude.
Find total photon number by dividing beam energy by energy per photon. Convert nm to m, mJ to J, and eV to J before using SI constants.
method: Convert data to compatible units.
Choose c = λν, E = hν, or the energy-level difference.
Keep atomic ΔE signed and photon energy positive.
units.trap: The n = 1 ground-state description here applies to hydrogen’s one electron; it is not a rule that all ground-state electrons in all atoms have n = 1.
units.label: Lecture 15

k: A quantum state whose probability density describes where an electron may be detected
Describes the relative size and energy of an orbital
Describes the shape of an orbital
Describes the spatial orientation of an orbital
Distinguishes two electrons in the same orbital (+½ or −½)
The wavelength associated with a moving particle
An intrinsic limit: position and momentum spreads obey ΔxΔp ≥ h/(4π)
units.title: Quantum numbers & matter waves
notes: An atomic orbital is a quantum state described by a wavefunction; its probability density tells us where the electron is likely to be detected. It is not a miniature planetary orbit.
Allowed values: n = 1,2,…; ℓ = 0,…,n − 1; mℓ = −ℓ,…,+ℓ; ms = +½ or −½. The labels s,p,d,f correspond to ℓ = 0,1,2,3.
A subshell has 2ℓ + 1 orbitals and holds up to 2(2ℓ + 1) electrons. A shell holds up to 2n² electrons.
A particle has de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p ≈ h/(mv) at nonrelativistic speed. The uncertainty relation ΔxΔp ≥ h/(4π) is intrinsic to quantum states, not just imperfect equipment.
method: Check whether every quantum number is allowed.
Count the possible orbitals and spin states.
For matter waves, use mass in kilograms.
units.trap: An impossible set of quantum numbers describes zero electrons, even if its individual numbers look familiar.
units.label: Lecture 16

k: No two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers
Electrons fill the lowest-energy available orbitals first
Equal-energy orbitals fill singly with parallel spins before pairing
For main-group atoms here: electrons in the outermost occupied principal shell
The listing of subshells and how many electrons each holds
f: Remove electrons from the highest-n orbitals first
Add electrons to the next available lowest-energy orbital
units.title: Electron configurations
notes: Fill available low-energy orbitals for the ground state. Each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins (Pauli).
Within a set of equal-energy orbitals, place one electron in each with parallel spins before pairing (Hund).
Count all electrons to identify an atom or ion. For main-group atoms, outermost-shell electrons are the valence electrons used in these exercises.

To form a cation, remove electrons from the highest principal shell first. Transition-metal cations lose ns electrons before (n−1)d electrons. Excited configurations need not follow ground-state filling order.
method: Determine the electron total from Z and charge.
Fill subshells and apply Hund’s rule.
Recount electrons and identify outermost-shell occupancy.
units.trap: The neutral filling sequence is not simply reversed to make a transition-metal cation.
units.label: Lecture 17

k: Energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom, forming a cation
Energies for removing the 1st, 2nd, 3rd… electrons one at a time
Energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron to form an anion
An atom’s tendency to pull shared electrons toward itself in a covalent bond
Atoms or ions with the same number of electrons
units.title: Periodic trends
notes: Across a period, increasing effective nuclear attraction generally pulls electrons closer. Atomic radius tends to decrease and first ionization energy tends to increase.
Down a group, extra shells and shielding usually increase radius and lower first ionization energy. These are patterns, not exception-free laws.
Cations are smaller than their parent atoms; anions are larger. In an isoelectronic series, more protons pull the same electron count into a smaller radius.

A large jump in successive ionization energies occurs when removal reaches a core electron. Electronegativity describes attraction for shared electrons, while electron affinity describes an energy change upon gaining an electron.
method: Check whether the comparison is within a period, group, or isoelectronic series.
Identify the change in shell count or nuclear charge.
Use the pattern with its physical reason.
units.trap: Do not rank arbitrary diagonal comparisons from arrows alone. Use data or a clearly justified comparison when trends compete.
units.label: Lecture 18

k: Electrostatic attraction between a cation and an anion
Positive ion formed when an atom loses electrons
Negative ion formed when an atom gains electrons
units.title: Ionic bonding
notes: Oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically. An ionic crystal is an extended arrangement of ions, not a collection of separate salt molecules.
A formula unit expresses the simplest neutral ratio of ions. Combine charges so the total is zero.
Main-group metals commonly lose valence electrons, and many nonmetals gain electrons. The resulting ions often have noble-gas electron counts.
The attraction in the crystal helps stabilize the ions. Electron transfer alone does not describe the entire energy balance of forming an ionic solid.
method: Predict or read the ion charges.
Choose the smallest ratio that balances charge.
Check the electron count of each ion.
units.trap: Ionic does not mean water-soluble. Solubility depends on the compound and conditions.
units.label: Lecture 19

k: Sharing of electrons between two atoms, typically nonmetals
Distance between two bonded nuclei, found at the minimum of the potential energy curve
Bond with electrons shared equally because the atoms have similar electronegativity
Bond with unequal sharing because the atoms differ in electronegativity
Symbols marking the electron-poor and electron-rich ends of a polar bond
units.title: Covalent bonds & bond polarity
notes: A covalent bond involves shared electron density between atoms. Unequal attraction for that density makes a bond polar.
The more electronegative bonded atom is the partial-negative end. A bond dipole points toward it; partial charge is not the same as an ion’s integer charge.
At the equilibrium bond length, potential energy is minimized and net force is zero. Very short separations are strongly repulsive.
Bonding lies on a continuum. Electronegativity differences are a useful guide, but a single rigid cutoff does not fully classify every compound.
method: Compare the bonded atoms’ electronegativities.
Place δ− on the more electronegative atom.
Separate bond polarity from whole-molecule polarity.
units.trap: A molecule can have polar bonds whose dipoles cancel. The supplied lectures establish bond polarity; whole-molecule geometry is an optional extension.
units.label: Lecture 19

k: Element symbol with dots for its valence electrons
Pair of valence electrons not shared in a bond
Main-group atoms tend to have 8 valence electrons (H and He: 2)
An atom, molecule, or ion with at least one unpaired electron
Central atom has fewer than 8 valence electrons, typically B or Al
A molecule represented with more than eight electrons around a period-3-or-heavier center
f: Electrons in single, double, triple bonds
Total valence electrons for an anion
Sum of atoms’ valence e⁻ + magnitude of the negative charge
Total valence electrons for a cation
Sum of atoms’ valence e⁻ − magnitude of the positive charge
units.title: Lewis structures & octet exceptions
notes: Count all valence electrons, adding for a negative charge and subtracting for a positive charge. Use two electrons per bond and per lone pair.
Choose connectivity, make single bonds, complete terminal octets, then allocate remaining electrons. Make multiple bonds if the central atom still lacks an octet.
Hydrogen needs only two electrons. Check both the total electron budget and each atom’s local electron count. Bracket a polyatomic ion and show its overall charge.
Lecture 20 explicitly includes odd-electron species, electron-deficient B/Al centers, and expanded-octet Lewis representations for period 3 or heavier centers.
method: Count the electron budget.
Build the skeleton and place pairs.
Check octets, charge, and any stated exception.
units.trap: A bond’s pair counts toward the octet of both bonded atoms, but counts only once in the molecule’s total electron budget.
units.label: Lectures 19–20, 22

k: Hypothetical atom charge assuming bonding electrons are shared equally
Several valid Lewis structures exist for the same arrangement of atoms
One of the individual Lewis structures of a resonant species
One delocalized electronic structure represented by multiple valid contributors
Electrons held by one atom or shared by just two
Electrons shared across three or more atoms
A full-headed curved arrow showing where one electron pair is reassigned
Valid contributors with the same energy by symmetry
A connected set of suitably aligned orbitals through which electrons can delocalize
f: FC = valence e⁻ − lone-pair e⁻ − ½(bonding e⁻)
FC = valence e⁻ − 2(lone pairs) − sum of bond orders
Equals the overall charge of the molecule or ion
Total bond-order contribution divided among equivalent bonds
units.title: Formal charge & resonance
notes: Formal charge assigns half the bonding electrons to each atom: FC = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − bond order sum.
Formal charges over the structure sum to the overall charge. Prefer reasonable octets and small charge separation; a negative formal charge usually favors a more electronegative atom.
Resonance contributors keep atom positions and connectivity fixed while changing electron placement. They are drawings of one delocalized structure, not separate molecules rapidly switching.
A lone pair adjacent to a π system may participate in delocalization when orbital alignment permits. Curved arrows start at electrons and indicate where that pair is placed.

A curved full-headed arrow begins at a lone pair or a bond and follows a pair of electrons to its destination. When a lone pair forms a new π bond, move the neighboring π pair if necessary to keep a second-period atom within an octet.
For equivalent contributors, shared bond order is intermediate. In carbonate, each C–O bond has an average order of 4/3; the molecule does not alternate between one long bond and one short bond.
An amide nitrogen lone pair can interact with the neighboring carbonyl π system when the orbitals align. An amine separated from a π bond by a saturated carbon has no continuous conjugated path.
method: Count nonbonding electrons and bond orders.
Compute every formal charge and check the total.
Compare valid contributors without moving atoms.
units.trap: Resonance moves electrons, not atoms. Preserve total charge and avoid placing more than eight electrons around a second-period atom.
units.label: Lectures 21–22

units.t: Strengths of Ionic and Covalent Bonds
k: Energy needed to break a covalent bond in the gas phase
Energy needed to break all bonds in a molecule into individual gaseous atoms
Here: positive energy required to separate an ionic solid into gaseous ions
Two routes to forming an ionic compound; Hess’s law finds an unknown step
f: ΔH°rxn = Σ D(bonds broken) − Σ D(bonds formed)
U = ΔHatom + ΣIE + ΔHdiss + ΣEA − ΔHf
units.title: Bond energies & lattice energy
notes: Breaking bonds requires energy; forming bonds releases it. Estimate a gas-phase reaction enthalpy as bond energies broken minus bond energies formed.
Average bond energies are approximate. Count every affected bond and multiply by its count. Different molecular environments can shift the exact value.
For the same pair of elements, a higher bond order usually means a shorter, stronger bond.
This app uses the positive lattice-dissociation convention: energy to separate a solid into gaseous ions. Larger charge magnitudes and smaller ion separations generally increase this energy.

Build a Born–Haber cycle from solid metal and elemental nonmetal in their reference states. Atomize the metal, ionize it to the required charge, dissociate the required amount of nonmetal, add electrons to gaseous atoms, and then assemble the crystal.

For MX₂ with M²⁺ and X⁻, include the first and second ionization energies, one X₂ dissociation, and two first electron affinities. A second electron affinity would add an electron to X⁻; it is not needed to make two separate X⁻ ions.
With positive lattice dissociation energy U, ΔHf = atomization + ionization + dissociation + electron affinity − U. If the question gives lattice formation enthalpy instead, its sign is negative.
method: List and count broken bonds.
List and count formed bonds.
Subtract formed-bond energy from broken-bond energy.
units.trap: Lattice formation energy has the opposite sign to lattice dissociation energy. Check the convention before comparing values.
units.label: Lecture 23

k: Electron domains around a central atom repel and arrange to minimize repulsion
A bond (single, double, or triple) or lone pair around a central atom
Arrangement of all domains, including lone pairs
Arrangement of the bonded atoms only
Vector sum of all bond dipoles in a molecule
A molecule with a nonzero net electric dipole moment
One of the two sites along the main axis in a trigonal bipyramid
One of the three sites in the central plane of a trigonal bipyramid
A bond directed out of the page toward the viewer
A bond directed behind the page away from the viewer
f: Electron domains on a central atom
# of bonded atoms + # of lone pairs
Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair (qualitative)
units.title: Molecular shape & polarity
notes: VSEPR counts electron domains around a central atom: each bonded atom gives one domain, and each lone pair gives one. A multiple bond still occupies one domain.
Electron geometry includes lone pairs. Molecular shape describes only the atom positions. Four domains give tetrahedral electron geometry, but lone pairs can produce pyramidal or bent shapes.
Lone pairs usually compress adjacent bond angles. In a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement, they preferentially occupy equatorial sites.
Molecular polarity is the vector sum of bond dipoles. Symmetry cancels them only when both arrangement and bonded-atom identities permit it.
Five domains give trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. Put lone pairs in equatorial positions first: AX₄E is seesaw, AX₃E₂ is T-shaped, and AX₂E₃ is linear.
Six domains give octahedral electron geometry. AX₅E is square pyramidal; for AX₄E₂, place the two lone pairs opposite one another to obtain a square-planar molecule.
A solid wedge projects toward the viewer; a hashed bond projects behind the page; an ordinary line lies in the page. These are perspective conventions, not different bond orders.

For molecules with several centers, determine the geometry around each center separately. Polar bonds cancel only when their vectors and magnitudes cancel; mixed terminal atoms can destroy an otherwise symmetric cancellation.
method: Count bonding domains and lone pairs.
Assign electron geometry, then molecular shape.
Check whether the bond dipoles cancel.
units.trap: A flat Lewis structure does not establish molecular polarity. Count domains, place lone pairs, and consider the identities and positions of the outer atoms.
units.label: Lectures 24–25

units.t: Valence Bond Theory, Hybrid Orbitals, and Multiple Bonds
units.title: Valence Bond Theory, Hybrid Orbitals, and Multiple Bonds
k: Bonding overlap along the line joining two nuclei
Bonding overlap of parallel orbitals on either side of the internuclear axis
A localized bonding model that combines orbitals on one atom into directional orbitals
A remaining p orbital available for side-on overlap in a π bond
The sign of an orbital wavefunction; matching phases can combine constructively. Colors do not indicate positive and negative electrical charge.
Hybrid orbitals in the same idealized set have equal energy.
A bookkeeping diagram that places an atom’s valence electrons into its hybrid orbitals and any remaining unhybridized orbitals.
f: sp: 2 hybrids + 2 p; sp²: 3 hybrids + 1 p; sp³: 4 hybrids
Course-model labels: 5 domains → sp³d; 6 domains → sp³d²
Number of atomic orbitals combined = number of hybrid orbitals formed
Localized sp² model: two paired sp² orbitals, one singly occupied sp² orbital, and one singly occupied p orbital
Count one σ bond for each connected atom pair, including bonds to hydrogen
notes: Count σ-bond directions and lone pairs around the selected atom. In the standard localized model, two, three, and four domains correspond to sp, sp², and sp³, with ideal arrangements of 180°, 120°, and 109.5°.
A multiple bond has one σ bond. Its additional π bonds come from side-on overlap of unhybridized p orbitals; those p orbitals must be aligned.
For an overlap question, identify both atoms and decide whether the requested bond is σ or π. An sp² carbon–hydrogen σ bond combines a carbon sp² orbital with a hydrogen 1s orbital.
Keep free-atom and bonded-atom orbital diagrams distinct. Free carbon has 2s²2p². A standard sp² valence-bond description uses three sp² orbitals and one p orbital for its four valence electrons.

Resonance can alter a simple domain-count assignment: an amide nitrogen is approximately planar and its lone pair occupies a p orbital that participates in conjugation. Use the displayed connectivity.
Orbital colors or plus/minus signs represent wavefunction phase, not ionic charge. Constructive overlap increases electron density between the nuclei; a node separates opposite-phase regions.
One s plus two p orbitals produces three sp² hybrids, leaving one p orbital. One s plus one p produces two sp hybrids and leaves two perpendicular p orbitals. The number of orbitals is conserved.
For five and six domains, the course uses the idealized labels sp³d and sp³d². Keep these model assignments distinct from the detailed electronic description of a real hypervalent molecule.

For a bonded-atom diagram, account for the atom’s assigned electrons, including formal charge. Reserve a singly occupied hybrid orbital for each σ bond and a singly occupied p orbital for each localized π bond; place remaining lone pairs in the appropriate orbitals.

In a simple carbonyl group, oxygen has two paired sp² orbitals and two singly occupied orbitals: one sp² for the σ bond and one p for the π bond. Carbon has three singly occupied sp² orbitals and one singly occupied p orbital.
Distinguish ideal electron-domain angles from measured molecular angles: tetrahedral domains have an ideal 109.5° angle; the H–O–H bond angle in water is approximately 104.5°.
method: Draw the local Lewis structure and identify the atom.
Count directions and identify σ versus π overlap.
Label hybrid orbitals, remaining p orbitals, and electron occupancy.
units.trap: Hybrid labels are model descriptions. A double bond counts as one domain but contains two bonds of different symmetry.
units.label: Lectures 26 & 28

units.title: Molecular Orbital Theory
k: An orbital whose occupation stabilizes the bonded arrangement relative to separated atoms
An orbital whose occupation opposes bonding, labeled with an asterisk
Half the difference between bonding and antibonding electron counts
Attracted to a magnetic field because at least one electron is unpaired
All electrons are paired; weakly repelled by a magnetic field
A region of zero wavefunction amplitude between the nuclei in an antibonding overlap.
A pair of π orbitals at the same energy; singly occupy both with parallel spins before pairing electrons.
An MO describes electrons across the molecule; a hybrid orbital is assigned to one atom in a localized bonding model.
f: Add electrons for negative charge; subtract for positive charge
Two compatible atomic orbitals combine to give two molecular orbitals: one bonding and one antibonding
Add one antibonding electron: bond order falls by 0.5; remove one: it rises by 0.5
notes: Count all valence electrons, adjusting for ionic charge. Occupy the molecular orbitals from low to high energy using Pauli exclusion and Hund’s rule.
For a degenerate pair of π orbitals, put one electron in each before pairing. Magnetism depends on the resulting unpaired electrons, not only on bond order.

Calculate bond order from all occupied bonding and antibonding orbitals in the stated diagram. A higher bond order generally corresponds to a shorter, stronger bond when comparing closely related species.
The order of σ2p and π2p levels is not universal. These practice questions state the required level order or give electron counts so that you do not have to guess a heteronuclear diagram.
An ion may lose an electron from a bonding or an antibonding orbital. Removing an antibonding electron raises bond order by one-half.
Combining two compatible atomic orbitals produces two MOs. The bonding combination places more density between the nuclei; the antibonding combination has a node between them.
The supplied CO practice diagram places π2p below σ2p. The supplied NF and CF practice diagrams place σ2p below π2p. Read the shown order instead of transferring one diagram to every species.

For helium species, fill σ1s before σ*1s. Four electrons give bond order zero in this elementary model; three give bond order one-half and one unpaired electron. Bond order zero means no net covalent stabilization in this model, rather than a universal claim that two atoms can never associate.
For a charged species, adjust the electron count first and refill the stated diagram. Decide magnetism from unpaired electrons after filling; do not infer it from the sign of the ion charge.
method: Count electrons with the charge included.
Fill the supplied MO order and check unpaired electrons.
Compute bond order from the occupied levels.
units.trap: Use the order supplied in the problem. An unpaired electron makes a species paramagnetic even if its bond order is an integer.

units.t: Gas Pressure and the Ideal Gas Law
units.title: Gas Pressure and the Ideal Gas Law
k: A model of particles with negligible volume and negligible intermolecular attractions
Temperature measured from absolute zero in kelvin
A container whose volume stays fixed
notes: Choose units before substitution. With R in L·atm/(mol·K), pressure must be in atm, volume in liters, amount in moles, and temperature in kelvin.
For a sealed rigid vessel, n and V are constant, so P/T is constant. Convert both temperatures to kelvin before comparing them.
For fixed n at constant temperature, pressure rises as volume decreases. At constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature.
PV = nRT applies to absolute pressure. If a problem gives a gauge reading, add the ambient pressure before using the ideal-gas equation.
method: List what stays constant.
Convert temperature to K and match R to the other units.
Solve symbolically, then substitute and report units.
units.trap: A ratio of Celsius temperatures is not a gas-law temperature ratio.
units.label: Summer Exam 4

units.title: Gas Density and Molar Mass
k: Mass of gas per unit volume under the stated conditions
Mass per mole averaged over the particles in a gas mixture
notes: Combine PV = nRT with n = m/M to obtain d = m/V = PM/(RT). This relates a measurable density to molar mass.
At fixed pressure and composition, warming a gas lowers its density because its particles occupy more volume per unit mass.
Use a consistent mass unit. For density in g/L and the L·atm gas constant, the molar mass comes out in g/mol.
The supplied Exam 4 tests density and molar-mass applications within §9.3. It does not establish complete lecture coverage of every mixture or gas-reaction subtopic in that section.
method: Identify P, T, density, and any known molar mass.
Rearrange d = PM/(RT).
For a second temperature, keep pressure and composition explicit.
units.trap: Density changes with temperature and pressure; molar mass does not change when the same gas is warmed.
units.label: Summer Exam 4

units.title: Effusion and the Kinetic-Molecular Theory
k: Escape of gas particles through a small opening into a lower-pressure region
Spreading and mixing due to molecular motion
Square root of the mean of squared molecular speeds
Average translational kinetic energy set by absolute temperature
f: urms = √(3RT / M), using M in kg/mol
notes: At the same temperature, gases have the same mean translational kinetic energy but different speed distributions. Lighter particles move faster on average.
The effusion-rate ratio varies with the inverse square root of molar mass. A gas that effuses twice as fast has one-quarter the molar mass.
For a fixed quantity passing through an opening, elapsed time is inversely proportional to effusion rate. Invert a time ratio before using it as a rate ratio.
Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and M in kg/mol for speed calculations. The resulting speed unit is m/s.

Mean speed and root-mean-square speed are different quantities. These questions name the statistic explicitly; the Exam 4 speed item is treated as an RMS-speed skill rather than copying its ambiguous “average velocity” wording.
method: Decide whether the quantity is rate, elapsed time, mean speed, or RMS speed.
Use kelvin and convert molar mass to kg/mol for speeds.
Check that the lighter gas is faster at the same temperature.
units.trap: Do not insert g/mol into √(3RT/M) with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
units.label: Summer Exam 4

units.title: Non-Ideal Gas Behavior
k: The van der Waals a term accounts for attractive interactions
The van der Waals b term accounts for finite particle size
Z = PV/(nRT); equals 1 for the ideal-gas model
notes: The ideal-gas model becomes less reliable when particles are crowded or attractions become important. Low pressure and sufficiently high temperature generally favor ideal behavior.

In a van der Waals description, a measures the attraction correction and b measures the excluded-volume correction. Under matching conditions, smaller corrections usually mean closer agreement with the ideal model.
Attractions tend to lower the measured pressure relative to the attraction-free picture. Finite particle volume reduces the space available for motion and tends to raise pressure.
The supplied exam compares gases using a and b. Comparisons must use the same conditions; the best match to ideal behavior cannot be decided from temperature or pressure alone.
method: Hold temperature, volume, and amount constant for comparisons.
Compare both attraction and excluded-volume corrections.
If calculating, match units and keep V greater than nb.
units.trap: Neither a nor b is a universal ideality score independent of conditions.

questions.prompt: Given Pd has [Kr] 4d¹⁰ and the Kr core includes 4s²4p⁶, how many electrons in Pd have n = 4?

questions.prompt: An electron has position uncertainty 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Use me = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Find the minimum speed uncertainty.

questions.prompt: How many total valence electrons are in CH₃C(=O)NH₂?

questions.prompt: In the standard expanded-octet Lewis structure of IF₄⁺, how many lone pairs are on iodine?

Opposite phase with a node between the nuclei

questions.prompt: An orbital diagram colors one lobe blue and the other red. What does the color difference normally represent?

steps: The colors distinguish phase, not electrical charge.
Both regions describe possible locations of a negatively charged electron.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.
options: Opposite signs of the orbital wavefunction
A positively charged lobe and a negatively charged lobe
A proton-filled lobe and an electron-filled lobe

questions.prompt: How many hybrid orbitals result when one s orbital and two p orbitals are combined?
steps: Three input orbitals produce three output orbitals.
The result is an sp² set; one of the original three p orbitals remains unhybridized.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: In the course’s idealized hybridization model, which label corresponds to six electron domains?
steps: Six domains correspond to an octahedral arrangement.
The course model labels the six-orbital set sp³d².
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: How many unhybridized p orbitals remain on each sp-hybridized carbon in a C≡C bond?
steps: One s and one p orbital are combined into two sp hybrids.
Two p orbitals remain; each participates in a different π overlap.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: How many σ bonds are present in CH₃–C≡C–CH₃? Include the C–H bonds.
steps: The six hydrogen atoms give six C–H σ bonds.
The four-carbon chain has three C–C connections, each with one σ bond.
Total σ bonds = 6 + 3 = 9. The triple bond also contains two π bonds.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: Which orbitals make the π bond of a simple C=C group?
questions.answer: One unhybridized p orbital on each carbon
steps: Each sp² carbon retains one unhybridized p orbital.
Parallel p orbitals overlap side-on to form the π interaction.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.
options: One unhybridized p orbital on each carbon
Two sp³ orbitals on each carbon
One hydrogen 1s orbital and one carbon sp² orbital

questions.prompt: What is the ideal angle between the directions of two sp hybrid orbitals?
steps: Two electron domains lie on opposite sides of the atom.
Their ideal linear arrangement has an angle of 180°.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: In the course model, a five-domain atom is assigned sp³d hybridization. How many hybrid orbitals are in that set?
steps: One s, three p, and one d orbital are combined in this idealized model.
Five input orbitals give five hybrid orbitals.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares ideal tetrahedral geometry and water?
questions.answer: The tetrahedral ideal is 109.5°; water’s H–O–H angle is about 104.5°
steps: Four electron domains lead to a tetrahedral reference arrangement.
The actual molecular angle need not equal the ideal domain angle; water is bent with an H–O–H angle near 104.5°.

Water has a linear 180° bond angle
Every molecule with two bonds has a 90° bond angle

questions.prompt: Combining two compatible 1s atomic orbitals produces how many molecular orbitals?
steps: The number of orbitals is conserved.
The combinations give one bonding σ1s MO and one antibonding σ*1s MO.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes σ*1s from σ1s in an elementary MO picture?
questions.answer: A node between the two nuclei
steps: The antibonding combination is formed by destructive interference between the nuclei.
The bonding combination instead increases electron density in that internuclear region.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.
options: A node between the two nuclei
A third nucleus in the center
An orbital that can hold four electrons
An orbital that must always be empty

questions.prompt: Use σ1s < σ*1s. What bond order does the elementary MO model predict for He₂?
steps: Two He atoms supply four electrons.
The occupancy is σ1s² σ*1s².
Bond order = (2 − 2)/2 = 0: there is no net covalent stabilization in this elementary model.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: Use σ1s < σ*1s. What bond order does the elementary MO model predict for He₂⁺?
steps: The two He atoms supply four electrons; the +1 charge removes one.
Occupancy is σ1s² σ*1s¹.
Bond order = (2 − 1)/2 = 0.5; one electron is unpaired.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: Under σ1s < σ*1s, what is the magnetic classification of He₂⁺?
steps: Three electrons occupy σ1s² σ*1s¹.
The singly occupied antibonding orbital makes the species paramagnetic.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.
options: Magnetism follows from positive charge alone

questions.prompt: For the stated order σ2s < σ*2s < π2p < σ2p < π*2p < σ*2p, find the bond order of CO⁺. Use C = 4 and O = 6 valence electrons.
steps: Valence electrons = 4 + 6 − 1 = 9.
Occupancy: σ2s² σ*2s² π2p⁴ σ2p¹.
There are seven bonding electrons and two antibonding electrons, so bond order = (7 − 2)/2 = 2.5 in this stated diagram.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: For σ2s < σ*2s < π2p < σ2p < π*2p < σ*2p, CO⁻ has 11 valence electrons. What is its magnetic classification?
questions.answer: Paramagnetic: one electron occupies the π* pair
steps: The first ten electrons fill σ2s² σ*2s² π2p⁴ σ2p².
The eleventh electron enters one π*2p orbital and remains unpaired.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.
options: Paramagnetic: one electron occupies the π* pair
Diamagnetic: the extra electron pairs in σ2p
Diamagnetic: all negatively charged ions have paired electrons

questions.prompt: NF has 12 valence electrons. Use σ2s < σ*2s < σ2p < π2p < π*2p < σ*2p. How many unpaired electrons result?
steps: Fill σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴, using ten electrons.
The last two enter the degenerate π* orbitals separately with parallel spins.
There are two unpaired electrons.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: NF⁻ has 13 valence electrons. Use σ2s < σ*2s < σ2p < π2p < π*2p < σ*2p. Calculate its bond order.
steps: Occupancy: σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴ π*2p³.
Bonding electrons = 2 + 2 + 4 = 8. Antibonding electrons = 2 + 3 = 5.
Bond order = (8 − 5)/2 = 1.5.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: Why does a simple Lewis structure fail to explain the paramagnetism of O₂?
questions.answer: It pairs all electrons, whereas the MO diagram has two unpaired electrons
steps: A standard O=O Lewis structure shows bonding and nonbonding electrons as pairs.
In the ground-state MO description, the two highest π* electrons occupy separate degenerate orbitals.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.
options: It pairs all electrons, whereas the MO diagram has two unpaired electrons
It gives oxygen the wrong atomic number
It predicts that every molecule is ionic
It assigns O₂ no valence electrons

questions.prompt: In a localized carbonyl-oxygen diagram, how are the six oxygen valence electrons placed in three sp² orbitals and one p orbital?
steps: Two lone pairs occupy two sp² orbitals.
One electron in the third sp² orbital contributes to the σ bond.
One electron in the unhybridized p orbital contributes to the π bond. Total = 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: A neutral carbonyl carbon forms three σ bonds and one π bond. Which bonded-atom valence-orbital occupancy fits?
steps: Carbon contributes four valence electrons.
Three singly occupied sp² orbitals provide σ overlap and one singly occupied p orbital provides π overlap.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: An amide-free nitrogen has two single bonds, two lone pairs, and formal charge −1. In the simple localized model, what is its hybridization?
steps: Two σ-bond directions plus two lone pairs make four electron domains.
The local assignment is sp³, with occupancies 2, 2, 1, 1.
The nitrogen is assigned six electrons in the localized bookkeeping: one more than a neutral nitrogen atom.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.
options: No hybrid orbitals because the atom is charged

questions.prompt: An oxygen has three single bonds, one lone pair, and formal charge +1. Which local hybrid-orbital occupancy is consistent?
steps: There are four domains: three σ bonds and one lone pair.
The oxygen is assigned five electrons, consistent with 6 − 1 for formal charge +1.
A paired orbital holds the lone pair; three singly occupied orbitals supply the σ bonds.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.
options: Four sp³ orbitals each containing two electrons
Three sp² orbitals all doubly occupied

questions.prompt: How many π bonds occur in CH₂=CH–C(=O)–CH₃?
steps: The C=C double bond supplies one π bond.
The C=O double bond supplies one π bond.
There are two π bonds total.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: How many σ bonds occur in CH₂=CH–C(=O)–CH₃? Include all bonds to H.
steps: There are six C–H bonds: two on CH₂, one on CH, and three on CH₃.
The four-carbon chain has three C–C σ bonds.
The C=O connection adds one C–O σ bond.
Total = 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 σ bonds.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.

questions.prompt: In CH₃–C(=O)–CH=CH₂, which orbitals overlap for the σ bond between the carbonyl carbon and the adjacent alkene carbon?
questions.answer: An sp² orbital on each carbon
steps: The carbonyl carbon has three σ-bond directions and is sp² in this model.
The adjacent alkene carbon also has three σ-bond directions and is sp².
The σ connection between them is an end-on sp²–sp² overlap.
questions.hint: Separate σ bonds, π bonds, and lone pairs.
options: An sp² orbital on each carbon
An sp³ orbital on each carbon

questions.prompt: CF⁺ has 10 valence electrons. Use σ2s < σ*2s < σ2p < π2p < π*2p < σ*2p. What is its bond order?
steps: Carbon contributes four valence electrons and fluorine seven; the +1 charge removes one.
Fill σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴.
Eight electrons are bonding and two are antibonding: bond order = (8 − 2)/2 = 3.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: CF has 11 valence electrons. Use σ2s < σ*2s < σ2p < π2p < π*2p < σ*2p. Which result follows?
steps: The first ten electrons fill σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴.
The eleventh occupies one π*2p orbital.
Bond order = (8 − 3)/2 = 2.5. One unpaired electron makes the species paramagnetic.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: CF⁻ has 12 valence electrons. Use σ2s < σ*2s < σ2p < π2p < π*2p < σ*2p. Which statement follows?
questions.answer: The two π* electrons are unpaired; bond order is 2
steps: Twelve valence electrons fill σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴ π*2p².
Hund’s rule puts the two π* electrons into separate orbitals with parallel spins.
Bond order = (8 − 4)/2 = 2; the species is paramagnetic.
questions.hint: Count the electrons, fill the stated energy order, then check bonding and unpaired electrons.
options: The two π* electrons are unpaired; bond order is 2
Both π* electrons pair immediately; bond order is 3
The extra electron enters σ*2p before π*2p
